In particular, hospitals are feeling the pain over a few commonly used IV fluids, including 50 and 100 ml. injection bags of sodium chloride (0.9% saline) and 5% dextrose. These fluids are key in keeping sick patients hydrated.

The reasons for the shortages are mostly related to manufacturing problems, BUT in many cases, some companies who make large portions of a drug, simply stop making it, OR a specific drug is only being produced by a single manufacturer. Explanation - There simply are not enough companies making the drug to keep up with the demand, and it's all part of a consolidation of the manufacturers who produce generic drugs.

That has caused US manufacturers to home-in on certain generics and discontinue others that don't make much money. AND if a generic manufacturer has a shortage, there's no easy fix - you can't pass off the job to another company while the first fixes its problems, since getting approval to take on a new drug can take years.

The AHA wants the FDA to push manufacturers that make these drugs to invest in creating more supplies in the future, as well as finding suppliers in the US that are not as susceptible to natural disasters.

It's not just IV fluids.

In 2007, 154 drugs were in shortage. This number almost tripled in 2012 and has increased every year. Threatening medical care and patients' lives, drug shortages have occurred in almost every pharmaceutical category - antibiotics, cancer drugs, anesthesia drugs, pain control, reproductive and gynecological, cardiac, and psychiatric have all been in varying degrees of short supply or not available at all. A few years,ago, nitroglycerine, an emergency room staple used to treat heart attack patients, was in such severe scarcity that its sole US manufacturer restricted hospitals to 40% of their usual orders.

Just last month, the AHA sent a letter to the FDA's commissioner, drawing attention to the large number of medications, especially those administered intravenously, that are facing shortages.

The main dining room, with striking murals of historic Philadelphia, recently closed to members and is now used primarily as a for-rent banquet facility. Members may use the squash courts at the Yale Club of New York City. Members also have access to more than 150 reciprocal private clubs worldwide. Today, the Penn Club has more than 5,000 members around the world. The Penn Club is controlled by its members and managed by third parties, although The University of Pennsylvania owns the clubhouse building and leases it to the Club.
